claim: Atg8 is a ubiquitin-like protein that plays central roles in autophagy in its lipidated form.
source: The ubiquitin-like protein Atg8, in its lipidated form, plays central roles in autophagy.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the autophagy field, supported by extensive prior research.

claim: Atg8 carries out lipidation-independent functions in non-autophagic processes.
source: Yet, remarkably, Atg8 also carries out lipidation-independent functions in non-autophagic processes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: In S. pombe and S. cerevisiae, the lipidation-independent roles of Atg8 in maintaining normal vacuole morphology and functions require its interaction with Hfl1.
source: Here we report that in the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe and the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the lipidation-independent roles of Atg8 in maintaining normal morphology and functions of the vacuole require its interaction with a vacuole membrane protein Hfl1 (homolog of human TMEM184 proteins).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing co-immunoprecipitation, localization studies, and phenotypic rescue experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Hfl1 is a homolog of human TMEM184 proteins.
source: Here we report that in the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe and the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the lipidation-independent roles of Atg8 in maintaining normal morphology and functions of the vacuole require its interaction with a vacuole membrane protein Hfl1 (homolog of human TMEM184 proteins).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The Atg8-Hfl1 interaction is not mediated by the typical Atg8-family-interacting motif (AIM) that forms an intermolecular β-sheet with Atg8.
source: Crystal structures revealed that the Atg8-Hfl1 interaction is not mediated by the typical Atg8-family-interacting motif (AIM) that forms an intermolecular β-sheet with Atg8.
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data presented in Figure 3 and described in the Results section.

claim: The Atg8-binding regions in Hfl1 proteins adopt a helical conformation.
source: Instead, the Atg8-binding regions in Hfl1 proteins adopt a helical conformation, thus representing a new type of AIMs (termed helical AIMs here).
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Helical AIMs represent a new type of Atg8-family-interacting motifs.
source: Instead, the Atg8-binding regions in Hfl1 proteins adopt a helical conformation, thus representing a new type of AIMs (termed helical AIMs here).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and comparison with canonical AIMs.

claim: Atg8 is conjugated to phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) through a series of enzymatic reactions.
source: Atg8 is conjugated to the membrane lipid phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) through a series of enzymatic reactions including its processing by the protease Atg4, activation by an E1-like enzyme Atg7, and covalent linking of its G116 residue to PE by the collaborative activities of an E2-like enzyme Atg3 and an E3-like complex Atg12–Atg5-Atg16 (Ichimura et al., 2000; Hanada et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Lipidated Atg8 on autophagic membranes is critically important for autophagosome formation.
source: Lipidated Atg8 on autophagic membranes is critically important for autophagosome formation (Kirisako et al., 1999), and also serves as a recruitment platform for selective autophagy receptors (Shintani et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Lipidated Atg8 serves as a recruitment platform for selective autophagy receptors.
source: Lipidated Atg8 on autophagic membranes is critically important for autophagosome formation (Kirisako et al., 1999), and also serves as a recruitment platform for selective autophagy receptors (Shintani et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The core consensus sequence of the AIM motif is W/F/YxxL/I/V.
source: The core consensus sequence of the AIM motif is the four-amino-acid sequence W/F/YxxL/I/V, in which 'x' denotes any amino acid.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: When bound to Atg8, the AIM motif adopts an extended β strand conformation and forms an intermolecular parallel β-sheet with the β2 strand of Atg8.
source: When bound to Atg8, this motif adopts an extended β strand conformation and forms an intermolecular parallel β-sheet with the β2 strand of Atg8.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The conserved aromatic residue (W/F/Y) in the AIM motif inserts into the W-site on Atg8.
source: The conserved aromatic residue (W/F/Y) and hydrophobic residue (L/I/V) in the AIM motif insert into two hydrophobic pockets on Atg8, termed the 'W-site' and the 'L-site', respectively (Noda et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The conserved hydrophobic residue (L/I/V) in the AIM motif inserts into the L-site on Atg8.
source: The conserved aromatic residue (W/F/Y) and hydrophobic residue (L/I/V) in the AIM motif insert into two hydrophobic pockets on Atg8, termed the 'W-site' and the 'L-site', respectively (Noda et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: In P. pastoris, the loss of Atg8 caused aberrant vacuole morphology, a phenotype not shared by atg7Δ and atg8-G116A mutants.
source: In the methylotrophic yeast Pichia pastoris, the loss of Atg8 caused aberrant vacuole morphology, a phenotype not shared by atg7Δ and atg8-G116A, two mutants defective in Atg8 lipidation (Mukaiyama et al., 2004; Tamura et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In S. pombe, the loss of Atg8 caused abnormal vacuole morphologies, including the formation of tubular-shaped vacuoles.
source: In another model yeast species, the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, the loss of Atg8 was also shown to cause abnormal vacuole morphologies, including the formation of tubular-shaped vacuoles, but the lipidation- and autophagy-deficient atg8-G116A mutant did not exhibit any vacuole morphology abnormalities (Mikawa et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In S. pombe, the lipidation- and autophagy-deficient atg8-G116A mutant did not exhibit any vacuole morphology abnormalities.
source: In another model yeast species, the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, the loss of Atg8 was also shown to cause abnormal vacuole morphologies, including the formation of tubular-shaped vacuoles, but the lipidation- and autophagy-deficient atg8-G116A mutant did not exhibit any vacuole morphology abnormalities (Mikawa et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Hfl1 was identified as a protein that specifically co-purified with Atg8-YFH in atg4Δ cells.
source: Among the proteins that specifically co-purified with Atg8-YFH is a protein called Hfl1 (systematic ID SPAC30D11.06c) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by AP-MS data presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Hfl1 is a vacuole membrane protein whose absence resulted in abnormal vacuole morphology.
source: Hfl1 was found in an unpublished study to be a vacuole membrane protein whose absence resulted in abnormal vacuole morphology (the name stands for 'Has Fused Lysosomes') (Lilavivat, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an unpublished study and confirmed by data in this manuscript.

claim: Hfl1 belongs to a conserved eukaryotic protein family (InterPro ID: IPR005178; PFAM ID: PF03619).
source: It belongs to a conserved eukaryotic protein family (InterPro ID: IPR005178; PFAM ID: PF03619, formerly DUF300).
evidence: This is based on database annotations and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Hfl1 is predicted to contain seven transmembrane helices followed by a C-terminal cytosolic tail.
source: Like other proteins in this family, Hfl1 is predicted to contain seven transmembrane helices followed by a C-terminal cytosolic tail (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction using PolyPhobius and shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In humans, members of the InterPro IPR005178 family include three TMEM184 proteins (TMEM184A, TMEM184B, and TMEM184C) and SLC51A.
source: In humans, members of this family include three TMEM184 proteins (TMEM184A, TMEM184B, and TMEM184C) and SLC51A (also known as organic solute transporter subunit alpha or OSTα).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TMEM184 proteins are more closely related to the fungal members of the InterPro IPR005178 family than SLC51A is.
source: The TMEM184 proteins are more closely related to the fungal members of this family than SLC51A is (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: SpHfl1 was co-immunoprecipitated with SpAtg8.
source: We confirmed that Atg8 interacts with Hfl1 in S. pombe using a co-immunoprecipitation analysis (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ScAtg8 was co-immunoprecipitated with ScHfl1.
source: To determine whether this interaction is conserved, we performed a co-immunoprecipitation analysis in S. cerevisiae, and found that the homolog of Hfl1 in S. cerevisiae, a previously uncharacterized protein YKR051W, can interact with S. cerevisiae Atg8 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SpHfl1 localized to the vacuole membrane.
source: In fission yeast, endogenously C-terminally GFP-tagged SpHfl1 localized to the vacuole membrane (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Endogenously N-terminally mYFP-tagged SpAtg8 exhibited both a cytosolic distribution and a faint but detectable vacuole membrane localization.
source: Endogenously N-terminally mYFP-tagged SpAtg8 exhibited both a cytosolic distribution and a faint but detectable vacuole membrane localization (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The vacuole membrane localization of mYFP-SpAtg8 was completely abolished in Sphfl1Δ cells.
source: The vacuole membrane localization of mYFP-SpAtg8 was completely abolished in Sphfl1Δ cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Overexpression of SpHfl1 resulted in the concentration of mYFP-SpAtg8 on the vacuole membrane.
source: Furthermore, when SpHfl1 was overexpressed from a strong nmt1 promoter, the cytosolic signal of mYFP-SpAtg8 disappeared and the vacuole membrane localization of mYFP-SpAtg8 became much more conspicuous (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: ScHfl1 localized to the vacuole membrane when overexpressed.
source: Using a strong TEF1 promoter to express ScHfl1, we found that like SpHfl1, it also localized to the vacuole membrane (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Overexpression of ScHfl1 resulted in the relocalization of ScAtg8 from the cytosol to the vacuole membrane.
source: Similar to the situation in fission yeast, the overexpression of ScHfl1 resulted in the relocalization of ScAtg8 from the cytosol to the vacuole membrane (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Loss of SpHfl1 in fission yeast did not affect starvation-induced autophagy.
source: Using CFP-SpAtg8 in fission yeast and GFP-ScAtg8 in budding yeast as reporters to monitor autophagy, we found that neither the loss of SpHfl1 in fission yeast nor the loss of ScHfl1 in budding yeast affected starvation-induced autophagy (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by autophagy assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Loss of ScHfl1 in budding yeast did not affect starvation-induced autophagy.
source: Using CFP-SpAtg8 in fission yeast and GFP-ScAtg8 in budding yeast as reporters to monitor autophagy, we found that neither the loss of SpHfl1 in fission yeast nor the loss of ScHfl1 in budding yeast affected starvation-induced autophagy (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by autophagy assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: DTT treatment resulted in the formation of tubular-shaped vacuoles in Spatg8Δ but not wild-type cells.
source: After testing a number of other stress-inducing conditions, we found that treating cells with the reducing agent dithiothreitol (DTT) resulted in the formation of tubular-shaped vacuoles in Spatg8Δ but not wild-type cells (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The tubular-shaped vacuole phenotype of Spatg8Δ was shared by Sphfl1Δ but not by Spatg1Δ, Spatg2Δ, Spatg3Δ, Spatg4Δ, Spatg5Δ, Spatg6Δ, Spatg7Δ, and Spatg8-G116A.
source: This phenotype of Spatg8Δ was shared by Sphfl1Δ but not by Spatg1Δ, Spatg2Δ, Spatg3Δ, Spatg4Δ, Spatg5Δ, Spatg6Δ, Spatg7Δ, and Spatg8-G116A (Figure 2A and B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), indicating that SpHfl1 and SpAtg8 act in a non-autophagic process to maintain normal vacuole morphology.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Spatg8Δ and Sphfl1Δ cells exhibited stronger sensitivity to ZnCl2, CoCl2, and MnCl2 than the wild type.
source: Among the metal salts we tested, which include NaCl, KCl, LiCl, MgSO4, CaCl2, ZnCl2, CoCl2, and MnCl2, Spatg8Δ and Sphfl1Δ cells exhibited stronger sensitivity to ZnCl2, CoCl2, and MnCl2 than the wild type (Figure 2C and data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by spot assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The metal sensitivity phenotype was not shared by the lipidation-defective mutants Spatg8-G116A, Spatg3Δ, and Spatg7Δ.
source: The metal sensitivity phenotype was not shared by the lipidation-defective mutants Spatg8-G116A, Spatg3Δ, and Spatg7Δ (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by spot assay data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The severity of the metal sensitivity phenotype was the same for Spatg8Δ and Sphfl1Δ, and the double mutant Spatg8Δ Sphfl1Δ did not show stronger phenotype than the two single mutants.
source: Notably, the severity of the metal sensitivity phenotype was the same for Spatg8Δ and Sphfl1Δ, and the double mutant Spatg8Δ Sphfl1Δ did not show stronger phenotype than the two single mutants (Figure 2C and D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), demonstrating that SpAtg8 and SpHfl1 act in the same pathway to confer normal metal tolerance.
evidence: This is supported by spot assay data shown in Figure 2C and D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Vacuolar microdomains were readily observed in wild-type but not Scatg8Δ cells at day 1 (D1) of the stationary phase.
source: We were able to reproduce this observation and found that vacuolar microdomains manifested as the reticular Vph1-mCherry pattern were readily observed in wild-type but not Scatg8Δ cells at day 1 (D1) of the stationary phase (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: The vacuolar microdomain formation phenotype of Scatg8Δ was shared by Schfl1Δ but not by Scatg1Δ and Scatg7Δ.
source: This phenotype of Scatg8Δ was shared by Schfl1Δ but not by Scatg1Δ and Scatg7Δ (Figure 2E and F), indicating that ScHfl1 and ScAtg8, but not ScAtg8 lipidation or autophagy, are important for vacuolar microdomain formation in cells cultured to D1 of the stationary phase.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: SpHfl1(1-269) was able to localize properly to the vacuole membrane but failed to recruit SpAtg8.
source: The N-terminal 7-transmembrane-helix region of SpHfl1, SpHfl1(1-269), when expressed from a plasmid in Sphfl1Δ cells, was able to localize properly to the vacuole membrane but failed to recruit SpAtg8 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), indicating that SpAtg8 recruitment requires the C-terminal cytosolic tail of SpHfl1.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: SpHfl1(1-410) retained the ability to recruit SpAtg8, whereas SpHfl1(1-385) and several shorter fragments lost the ability.
source: We then examined a series of C-terminally truncated versions of SpHfl1, and found that SpHfl1(1-410), which lacks the last 16 amino acids, retained the ability to recruit SpAtg8, whereas SpHfl1(1-385) and several shorter fragments lost the ability (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), indicating that the region between amino acids 385 and 410 is critical for SpAtg8 recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: SpHfl1Δ(386-409) failed to recruit SpAtg8.
source: Consistent with this idea, SpHfl1Δ(386-409), which lacks 24 amino acids, also failed to recruit SpAtg8 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Only SpHfl1(1-410) was able to complement the vacuole morphology defect of Sphfl1Δ.
source: Using the same set of plasmids to complement the vacuole morphology defect of Sphfl1Δ, we found that only SpHfl1(1-410) was able to complement (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that the SpAtg8-recruitment ability of SpHfl1 is important for maintaining normal vacuole morphology.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: SpHfl1(1-410) but not SpHfl1(1-385) or SpHfl1Δ(386-409) was able to co-immunoprecipitate SpAtg8.
source: Supporting this idea, we found that SpHfl1(1-410) but not SpHfl1(1-385) or SpHfl1Δ(386-409) was able to co-immunoprecipitate SpAtg8 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The cytosolic tail region, SpHfl1(270-426), was sufficient for co-immunoprecipitating SpAtg8.
source: Furthermore, the cytosolic tail region, SpHfl1(270-426), was sufficient for co-immunoprecipitating SpAtg8 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: SpHfl1(386-409) could efficiently pull down recombinant SpAtg8 but not a control protein Yng2-PHD.
source: We synthesized an SpHfl1(386-409) peptide and performed in vitro pull-down analysis. SpHfl1(386-409) could efficiently pull down recombinant SpAtg8 but not a control protein Yng2-PHD (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by peptide pull-down data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: SpHfl1(386-409) could pull down ScAtg8 as efficiently as SpAtg8.
source: Using the same assay, we found that SpHfl1(386-409) could pull down ScAtg8 as efficiently as SpAtg8 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C), despite that this region of SpHfl1 is not well conserved in ScHfl1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by peptide pull-down data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The crystal structure of SpAtg8 complexed with SpHfl1(386-409) was solved at 2.2 Å resolution.
source: To understand the atomic details of the SpHfl1-SpAtg8 interaction, we solved the crystal structure of SpAtg8 complexed with SpHfl1(386-409) at 2.2 Å resolution (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2E, and Supplementary file 2—Table S1).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data presented in Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2E, and Supplementary file 2—Table S1.

claim: The structure of SpAtg8 can be superimposed on that of ScAtg8 with an rms difference of 0.8 Å for main-chain atoms except for those of terminal tails.
source: The structure of SpAtg8 can be superimposed on that of ScAtg8 with an rms difference of 0.8 Å for main-chain atoms except for those of terminal tails (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F.

claim: SpHfl1(386-409) is comprised of an extended coil followed by an α-helix.
source: SpHfl1(386-409) is comprised of an extended coil followed by an α-helix, and interacts with the W-site, the L-site, as well as α3 of SpAtg8, burying ~2000 Å2 of surface area (detailed interactions are summarized in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 3A and B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: SpHfl1(386-409) interacts with the W-site, the L-site, as well as α3 of SpAtg8, burying ~2000 Å2 of surface area.
source: SpHfl1(386-409) is comprised of an extended coil followed by an α-helix, and interacts with the W-site, the L-site, as well as α3 of SpAtg8, burying ~2000 Å2 of surface area (detailed interactions are summarized in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 3A and B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: SpHfl1(386-409) neither forms an intermolecular β-sheet with β2 of Atg8.
source: Strikingly, SpHfl1(386-409) neither forms an intermolecular β-sheet with β2 of Atg8 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G, middle), nor uses two hydrophobic residues separated by two residues to engage the W-site and the L-site.
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2G.

claim: SpHfl1(386-409) uses Phe388 at the coil and Tyr398 at the helix for binding to the W-site and the L-site, respectively, with as many as nine residues between them.
source: Instead, SpHfl1(386-409) uses Phe388 at the coil and Tyr398 at the helix for binding to the W-site and the L-site, respectively, with as many as nine residues between them (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: The crystal structure of ScHfl1(368-389)-ScAtg8 fusion protein was determined at 2.45 Å resolution.
source: The crystal structure of ScHfl1(368-389)-ScAtg8 fusion protein was determined at 2.45 Å resolution (Figure 3—figure supplement 2I and Supplementary file 2—Table S1).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2I and Supplementary file 2—Table S1.

claim: ScHfl1(368-389) has an elongated conformation with a short helical conformation at the residues 374–377.
source: ScHfl1(368-389) has an elongated conformation with a short helical conformation at the residues 374–377, and forms extensive interactions with the W-site, the L-site, α3, as well as β3 of ScAtg8, burying ~2400 Å2 of surface area (detailed interactions are summarized in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 3C and D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: ScHfl1(368-389) forms extensive interactions with the W-site, the L-site, α3, as well as β3 of ScAtg8, burying ~2400 Å2 of surface area.
source: ScHfl1(368-389) has an elongated conformation with a short helical conformation at the residues 374–377, and forms extensive interactions with the W-site, the L-site, α3, as well as β3 of ScAtg8, burying ~2400 Å2 of surface area (detailed interactions are summarized in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 3C and D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: ScHfl1 neither forms an intermolecular β-sheet with Atg8 β2.
source: As is the case with SpHfl1, ScHfl1 neither forms an intermolecular β-sheet with Atg8 β2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G, bottom), nor uses a canonical AIM sequence for binding to the W-site and the L-site.
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2G.

claim: ScHfl1(368-389) uses Trp371 at the coil and Ile375 at the short helix for binding to the W-site and the L-site, respectively, with three residues between them.
source: Instead, ScHfl1(368-389) uses Trp371 at the coil and Ile375 at the short helix for binding to the W-site and the L-site, respectively, with three residues between them (Figure 3E and F, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 3E and F, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Tyr387 of ScHfl1 binds to a hydrophobic pocket formed between α3 and β3 of ScAtg8.
source: Unexpectedly, Tyr387 of ScHfl1 binds to a hydrophobic pocket formed between α3 and β3 of ScAtg8. This pocket, which has never been reported to be a binding site for AIMs, is named 'Y-site' because it accommodates a conserved Tyr residue in Hfl1.
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The Y-site has never been reported to be a binding site for AIMs.
source: This pocket, which has never been reported to be a binding site for AIMs, is named 'Y-site' because it accommodates a conserved Tyr residue in Hfl1.
evidence: This is based on a review of the literature and the novelty of the finding.

claim: SpHfl1(386-413) and ScHfl1(362-391) showed Kd values of 161 nM and 1.38 μM to SpAtg8 and ScAtg8, respectively.
source: SpHfl1(386-413) and ScHfl1(362-391), which encompass the Atg8-binding regions in the crystal structures, showed Kd values of 161 nM and 1.38 μM to SpAtg8 and ScAtg8, respectively (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The affinities of SpHfl1 and ScHfl1 for Atg8 are strong compared with canonical AIMs that typically show a Kd value of 1–100 μM.
source: These affinities, especially that of SpHfl1, are strong compared with canonical AIMs that typically show a Kd value of 1–100 μM (Zaffagnini and Martens, 2016).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published data on canonical AIMs.

claim: Alanine-substitution of SpHfl1 Phe388 (F388A) resulted in ~4 fold decrease in the affinity with SpAtg8.
source: Alanine-substitution of SpHfl1 Phe388 (F388A) and Tyr398 (Y398A), which bind to the W-site and the L-site in SpAtg8, resulted in ~4 fold and ~1000 fold decrease in the affinity with SpAtg8, respectively (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Alanine-substitution of SpHfl1 Tyr398 (Y398A) resulted in ~1000 fold decrease in the affinity with SpAtg8.
source: Alanine-substitution of SpHfl1 Phe388 (F388A) and Tyr398 (Y398A), which bind to the W-site and the L-site in SpAtg8, resulted in ~4 fold and ~1000 fold decrease in the affinity with SpAtg8, respectively (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Binding to the L-site is much more important than that to the W-site for the SpHfl1-SpAtg8 interaction.
source: This result suggests that binding to the L-site is much more important than that to the W-site for the SpHfl1-SpAtg8 interaction, which is in contrast to the interactions between canonical AIMs and Atg8 where the W-site binding is usually more important than the L-site binding (Noda et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the ITC data showing differential effects of F388A and Y398A mutations.

claim: ScHfl1 W371A mutation showed a much more pronounced reduction in affinity with ScAtg8 (~170 fold) than the I375A mutation (~13 fold).
source: In this regard, ScHfl1 is more similar to canonical AIMs than SpHfl1: ScHfl1 uses Trp371 and Ile375 for binding to the W-site and the L-site, respectively, and the W371A mutation showed a much more pronounced reduction in affinity with ScAtg8 (~170 fold) than the I375A mutation (~13 fold) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Alanine substitution of Tyr387 and Asp384 in ScHfl1 showed ~5 fold and ~7 fold reduction in affinity, respectively.
source: Besides the residues binding to the canonical binding surfaces of Atg8, alanine substitution of Tyr387 and Asp384 in ScHfl1, which bind to the Y-site and Arg65 of Atg8, showed ~5 fold and ~7 fold reduction in affinity, respectively (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The Y398A mutation in SpHfl1 completely abolished the SpAtg8-recruitment ability.
source: The point mutation that had the strongest effect in the in vitro ITC analysis, Y398A, completely abolished the SpAtg8-recruitment ability and strongly diminished the ability to complement the vacuole morphology phenotype of Sphfl1Δ.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4B–D.

claim: SpHfl1(Y398A) lost the ability to complement the metal sensitivity phenotype of Sphfl1Δ.
source: Furthermore, we found that SpHfl1(Y398A) lost the ability to complement the metal sensitivity phenotype of Sphfl1Δ (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by spot assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Fusing SpHfl1 and SpAtg8 to the same mCherry protein restored the ability of SpHfl1(Y398A) to complement Sphfl1Δ.
source: We found that such a fusion restored the ability of SpHfl1(Y398A) to complement Sphfl1Δ (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2), thus demonstrating that the phenotypic consequences of the Y398A mutation mainly result from a disruption of the SpHfl1-SpAtg8 binding.
evidence: This is supported by spot assay and microscopy data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The physical association between SpHfl1 and SpAtg8 is essential for the lipidation-independent vacuolar functions of SpAtg8.
source: Together, these results indicate that the physical association between SpHfl1 and SpAtg8 is essential for the lipidation-independent vacuolar functions of SpAtg8.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutational analysis and rescue experiments.

claim: Neither fusion of SpAtg8 to Hmt1 nor fusion to Zhf1 was able to rescue the vacuole morphology phenotype of Sphfl1Δ.
source: Neither fusion to the vacuolar phytochelatin transporter Hmt1 nor fusion to the vacuolar zinc transporter Zhf1 was able to rescue the vacuole morphology phenotype of Sphfl1Δ (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), suggesting that SpHfl1 may have role(s) beyond recruiting SpAtg8 to the vacuole membrane.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The W371A, I375A, D384A, and Y387A mutations each strongly diminished the ability of TEF1-promoter-expressed ScHfl1 to recruit ScAtg8 to the vacuole membrane.
source: In budding yeast, consistent with the ITC results, the W371A, I375A, D384A, and Y387A mutations each strongly diminished the ability of TEF1-promoter-expressed ScHfl1 to recruit ScAtg8 to the vacuole membrane (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: None of the W371A, I375A, D384A, and Y387A mutations individually had an obvious effect on the ability of ScHfl1 to complement the microdomain formation defect of Schfl1Δ.
source: Surprisingly, none of these mutations individually had an obvious effect on the ability of ScHfl1 expressed from either the strong TEF1 promoter or the weak URA3 promoter to complement the microdomain formation defect of Schfl1Δ (Figure 4G and H, and Figure 4—figure supplement 4), suggesting that the residual Atg8-binding ability is sufficient for the microdomain formation function.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4G and H, and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Combining W371A, I375A, D384A, and Y387A together led to the complete loss of the ability of ScHfl1 to complement Schfl1Δ.
source: To further reduce the ScAtg8-binding ability of ScHfl1, we combined mutations together and found that combining W371A and I375A to simultaneously disrupt the interactions at the W-site and the L-site was not able to abolish the ability of ScHfl1 to complement Schfl1Δ, whereas combining W371A, I375A, D384A, and Y387A together led to the complete loss of the complementing ability (Figure 4G and H, and Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4G and H, and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The quadruple mutant ScHfl1(W371A I375A D384A Y387A) showed no binding with ScAtg8.
source: We confirmed by ITC measurements that the double mutant (W371A I375A) retained weak affinity, but that the quadruple mutant (W371A I375A D384A Y387A) showed no binding with ScAtg8 (Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The ability of ScHfl1(W371A I375A D384A Y387A) to complement Schfl1Δ was restored by fusing it with ScAtg8.
source: The ability of ScHfl1(W371A I375A D384A Y387A) to complement Schfl1Δ was restored by fusing it with ScAtg8 (Figure 4J), indicating that the microdomain formation defect of this ScHfl1 mutant is indeed due to a loss of ScAtg8-binding ability.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The physical interaction between Atg8 and Hfl1 is vitally important to the lipidation-independent vacuolar functions of Atg8 in S. pombe and S. cerevisiae.
source: In sum, our results showed that the physical interaction between Atg8 and Hfl1 is vitally important to the lipidation-independent vacuolar functions of Atg8 in these two model yeast species.
evidence: This is inferred from the comprehensive mutational analysis and rescue experiments.

claim: Helical AIMs do not conform to the two common features of canonical AIMs/LIRs.
source: The helical AIMs we identified in SpHfl1 and ScHfl1 do not conform to these rules: they do not form an intermolecular β-sheet with Atg8 and they do not have a W/F/YxxL/I/V motif.
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data.

claim: SpHfl1 and ScHfl1 respectively use FxxxxxxxxxY and WxxxI sequences for Atg8 binding.
source: Instead, SpHfl1 and ScHfl1 respectively use FxxxxxxxxxY and WxxxI sequences for Atg8 binding.
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data.

claim: The larger numbers of intervening residues between the two hydrophobic residues in helical AIMs are possible because helical AIMs do not have to form an intermolecular β-sheet.
source: The larger numbers of intervening residues between the two hydrophobic residues are possible because helical AIMs do not have to form an intermolecular β-sheet—if an intermolecular β-sheet is formed, the number of intervening residues must be strictly two.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis.

claim: TMEM184A localizes to endosomes in mouse Sertoli cells and is required for the normal localization of the plasma membrane SNARE protein Stx2.
source: TMEM184A (also called Sdmg1) localizes to endosomes in mouse Sertoli cells and is required for the normal localization of the plasma membrane SNARE protein Stx2 (Best et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: TMEM184A acts as a heparin receptor in vascular cells and regulates angiogenesis.
source: TMEM184A also acts as a heparin receptor in vascular cells and regulates angiogenesis (Farwell et al., 2017; Pugh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TMEM184B localizes to recycling endosomes in mouse neurons and is important for the maintenance of synaptic architecture.
source: TMEM184B localizes to recycling endosomes in mouse neurons and is important for the maintenance of synaptic architecture (Bhattacharya et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In Arabidopsis thaliana, two TMEM184-related proteins, LAZ1 and LAZ1H1, localize to the vacuole membrane and are redundantly required for normal vacuole morphology and functions.
source: In the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana, two TMEM184-related proteins, LAZ1 and LAZ1H1, localize to the vacuole membrane and are redundantly required for normal vacuole morphology and functions (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Yeast Hfl1 proteins and their closest homologs in animals and plants share a common attribute of localizing to either endosomal or lysosomal compartments.
source: Thus, yeast Hfl1 proteins and their closest homologs in animals and plants share a common attribute of localizing to either endosomal or lysosomal compartments, but whether they share a common function remains to be determined.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization data for Hfl1 and its homologs.

claim: SLC51A/OSTα proteins bind to the single-transmembrane SLC51B/OSTβ proteins and transport bile acids and steroids at the plasma membrane.
source: More distantly related to the yeast Hfl1 proteins but belonging to the same InterPro IPR005178 protein family are the animal SLC51A/OSTα proteins, which bind to the single-transmembrane SLC51B/OSTβ proteins and transport bile acids and steroids at the plasma membrane (Ballatori et al., 2013; Dawson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The InterPro IPR005178 family proteins may not necessarily all be transporters.
source: However, a recent phylogenetic study has grouped TMEM184 proteins and SLC51A proteins into the transporter–opsin–GPCR (TOG) superfamily, which includes non-transporter proteins such as the G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) (Saier et al., 2016; Yee et al., 2013), hinting that the InterPro IPR005178 family proteins may not necessarily all be transporters.
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic analysis cited from prior research.

claim: Hfl1, as a GPCR-like transmembrane protein on the vacuole membrane, could play a sensing role to monitor changes occurring inside the vacuole lumen.
source: It is possible that Hfl1, as a GPCR-like transmembrane protein on the vacuole membrane, could play a sensing role to monitor changes occurring inside the vacuole lumen, and Atg8 may facilitate signal transduction in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the structural similarity to GPCRs.

claim: The two vacuole-related phenotypes of Spatg8Δ and Sphfl1Δ mutants—metal sensitivity and abnormal vacuole morphology—may share the same underlying cause.
source: The two vacuole-related phenotypes of Spatg8Δ and Sphfl1Δ mutants—metal sensitivity and abnormal vacuole morphology—may share the same underlying cause, as the same perturbation of vacuole organization or function may reduce the ability of this organelle to sequester metals, and at the same time, alter its morphology.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed phenotypes.

claim: A substantial fraction of deletion mutants sensitive to metals in S. cerevisiae are those exhibiting abnormal vacuole morphology.
source: Consistent with this idea, genome-wide deletion library screens in S. cerevisiae have shown that a substantial fraction of deletion mutants sensitive to metals are those exhibiting abnormal vacuole morphology (Pagani et al., 2007; Ruotolo et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The only other genetic perturbation that can result in tubular vacuoles in fission yeast is the overexpression of the dynamin homolog Vps1.
source: To our knowledge, the only other genetic perturbation that can result in tubular vacuoles in fission yeast is the overexpression of the dynamin homolog Vps1 (Röthlisberger et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on a review of the literature.

claim: vps1Δ suppressed the tubular vacuole phenotype of Spatg8Δ.
source: Furthermore, vps1Δ suppressed the tubular vacuole phenotype of Spatg8Δ (Mikawa et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: SpAtg8 and SpHfl1 may directly or indirectly restrain the vacuole tubulation activity of Vps1.
source: Thus, SpAtg8 and SpHfl1 may directly or indirectly restrain the vacuole tubulation activity of Vps1.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic interaction data.

claim: The microdomain formation defect of Scatg8Δ and Schfl1Δ mutants indicates that ScAtg8 and ScHfl1 contribute to the stationary-phase-induced vacuole membrane partitioning process.
source: The microdomain formation defect of Scatg8Δ and Schfl1Δ mutants indicates that ScAtg8 and ScHfl1 contribute to the stationary-phase-induced vacuole membrane partitioning process (Toulmay and Prinz, 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the observed phenotypes and cited prior research.

claim: In Drosophila, a form of noncanonical autophagy required for programmed midgut removal is dependent on Atg8 but not Atg7 and Atg3.
source: In Drosophila, a form of noncanonical autophagy required for programmed midgut removal is dependent on Atg8 but not Atg7 and Atg3, the E1 and E2 proteins needed for Atg8 lipidation (Chang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In mammalian cells, the formation of ERAD tuning vesicle/EDEMosome depends on non-lipidated LC3.
source: In mammalian cells, a non-autophagic process, the formation of ERAD tuning vesicle/EDEMosome, depends on non-lipidated LC3, but the exact mechanism is unclear (Calì et al., 2008; Reggiori et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Interactions between Atg8 and a transmembrane protein may underlie lipidation-independent functions of Atg8 in animals.
source: Our findings on the lipidation-independent vacuolar functions of Atg8 in yeasts suggest the possibility that interactions between Atg8 and a transmembrane protein may underlie these lipidation-independent functions of Atg8 in animals.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the findings in yeast.
